identity.title: Neon: Negative Extrapolation From Self-Training Improves Image Generation

problem.claim: High-quality training data is scarce, motivating synthetic-data augmentation for generative-model fine-tuning.

gap.claim: Self-training with synthetic data can trigger model autophagy disorder/model collapse, rapidly degrading sample quality or diversity.

contributions.claim: Introduces Neon, which fine-tunes on self-synthesized data and then reverses gradient updates to extrapolate away from degraded weights.
Provides an explanation based on anti-alignment between synthetic and real-data population gradients caused by typical high-probability-favoring samplers.

Reports a simple post-hoc merge requiring no new real data, operating with as few as 1k synthetic samples and typically under 1% additional training compute, across multiple model families and datasets.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors characterize Neon as a new learning method that converts self-training degradation into a signal for self-improvement.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that Neon works with as few as 1k synthetic samples and typically uses less than 1% additional training compute.
The authors report applicability across diffusion, flow-matching, autoregressive, and inductive moment-matching models on ImageNet, CIFAR-10, and FFHQ.
On ImageNet 256×256, the authors report an FID of 1.02 for xAR-L with 0.36% additional training compute, described as a new state of the art.

narrative_sequence.summary: Training-data scarcity motivates augmenting real data with synthetic data.
Synthetic self-training can create a positive feedback loop that causes model collapse and harms quality or diversity.
Neon reverses post-self-training gradient updates; the authors attribute this to correcting sampler-induced gradient anti-alignment.
The method is presented as lightweight and broadly applicable, with a reported ImageNet FID of 1.02 for xAR-L.

source_observation.claim: The abstract pairs a counterintuitive optimization operation with a mechanism explaining why degradation may provide a useful signal.

lessons.interpretation: A surprising intervention is more persuasive when its direction and rationale are stated together.
lessons.application: When presenting an unconventional update rule, connect the operation directly to a measurable failure mode and an explicit explanatory mechanism.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when no mechanism is available or when the abstract cannot support the proposed explanation.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify proof assumptions or the exact theoretical guarantees.
Comparative baselines, training protocols, and uncertainty for the reported FID and compute results are not given.
The meaning of “new state of the art” is author-reported; the comparison set is unspecified.
